text: Single-qubit gates are useful, but the real power of quantum computing shows up the moment two or more qubits start interacting. This lesson builds the single most important two-qubit circuit in the field — the Bell state.

The controlled-X gate, qc.cx of control and target, flips the target qubit only if the control qubit is |1>. Control and target order matters: cx(0,1) and cx(1,0) are genuinely different circuits. Applied to a qubit already in superposition, this conditional behavior is exactly what creates entanglement.

h(0) puts qubit 0 into an equal superposition. cx(0,1) then says: if qubit 0 is 1, flip qubit 1. Because qubit 0 is in superposition rather than a definite value, this entangles the two qubits into a single combined state rather than two independent ones.

The resulting state is exactly the sum of |00> and |11>, divided by the square root of 2 — a superposition over only two of the four possible outcomes. That gives ideal probabilities P(00)=0.5, P(11)=0.5, and exactly zero on 01 and 10. Once you measure qubit 0 and get, say, 1, you know with absolute certainty qubit 1 is also 1 — there's no way to ever observe 01 or 10 from this circuit.

A real seeded run at 1024 shots gives something like 00: 503, 11: 521, 01: 0, 10: 0. The 503-versus-521 split is ordinary shot noise, the same kind you saw with a single qubit. But 01 and 10 aren't close to zero — they are exactly zero, every single time, because the Bell state has genuinely zero amplitude there. Don't mistake a true structural zero for a result that merely happened to land on zero this time.

Next lesson trades a fixed numeric angle for something more flexible — a symbolic Parameter that lets you build a circuit template once and bind many different values to it, exactly the pattern Chapter 6's variational algorithms are built on.
